PAGE 1: Overview

OVERVIEW
========

Children have rights that protect their lives, their schooling and their safety. They also have responsibilities. In this sub-strand you will name forms of child abuse, explain causes and effects, and learn how to protect yourself and other children.

## Strand 5.0: Citizenship and Governance in Kenya
Sub-strand 5.3: Child Rights
Suggested lessons: 4

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) outline forms of child abuse in the community
b) explain the causes of child abuse in the community
c) explain effects of child abuse in the community
d) desire to promote child rights and responsibilities in the school

## What this sub-strand covers
• Early and forced marriages
• Female genital mutilation
• Slavery
• Child trafficking
• Child/forced labour
• Sexual abuse
• Abuse of children with special needs
• Unauthorised school transport

## Key inquiry questions
1. How can harmful cultural practices violate child rights in the community?
2. How can we protect ourselves from child abuse?

## Core competencies
• Self-Efficacy: Learners participate in activities that promote child rights in the school

## Values
• Responsibility: Learners design posters on the effects of child abuse in the community

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Gender Issues: Learners identify the causes of child abuse in the community.

## Links to other learning areas
• Religious Education: Learners participate in activities that promote child rights in the school.

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 Social Studies Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Strand 5.0 Citizenship and Governance in Kenya, Sub-strand 5.3 Child Rights
• KICD Grade 4 Social Studies radio lesson: Child Abuse in the Community
• Children Act, Kenya; Childline Kenya helpline 116

PAGE 2: Lesson 1: Rights and forms of child abuse

LESSON 1: RIGHTS AND FORMS OF CHILD ABUSE
=========================================

## What you will learn
• State basic rights and responsibilities of a child.
• Outline the forms of child abuse in the community.

Curriculum outcomes: a) outline forms of child abuse in the community; d) desire to promote child rights and responsibilities in the school

## Introduction
A child who is in school, has a name, and can tell a trusted adult when something is wrong is living some of the rights children are owed. Abuse is what happens when those rights are broken.

## Notes
A right is something a person is owed so that they can live with dignity. In Kenya, children have rights that include a name, education, health care, food and shelter, play, and protection from harm. A child is a person under 18 years.

Rights come with responsibilities. A responsibility is your part. Children should respect parents, teachers and other children, work hard at school, care for property, and tell a trusted adult about harm.

Child abuse is harming a child in a physical, sexual or emotional way. It is a crime. These are forms you should be able to outline:

- Early and forced marriage: a child is made to marry instead of staying in school. Marriage of a child is unlawful in Kenya.
- Female genital mutilation: cutting the private parts of a girl. It injures girls and is against the law. It is sometimes called female circumcision. The lawful name of the harm is female genital mutilation.
- Slavery: a child is handed over to work hard without pay, sometimes after an adult has been given money.
- Child trafficking: a child is stolen or moved and sold, inside Kenya or to another country, so that someone else can use them.
- Child labour or forced labour: a child is made to work for money instead of going to school, for example in a quarry or as a house help.
- Sexual abuse: an adult forces a child into sexual acts, or forces a child into marriage. Tell a trusted adult. You do not have to describe details to your friends.
- Abuse of children with special needs: hiding them, locking them away, refusing them play, or refusing them movement and school.
- Unauthorised school transport: putting learners into vehicles the school has not approved, including lifts from strangers.

Both girls and boys can be abused. Helping work at home after school, matched to your age, is not the same as child labour. Labour replaces school or is dangerous and forced.

## Key words
• right — something a person is owed so that they can live with dignity
• child abuse — harming a child physically, sexually or emotionally
• child labour — forcing a child to work instead of going to school

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A 12-year-old is kept at home every day to work as a house help for pay. Which form of abuse is this?

Working:
1. The child is not in school.
2. The work is for money and replaces education.

Answer: Child labour.

### Example 2
A girl is told she will be cut during a ceremony and then married. Which forms of abuse are these?

Working:
1. Cutting girls' private parts is female genital mutilation.
2. Marrying a child is early and forced marriage.

Answer: Female genital mutilation and early or forced marriage.

## Activity: Outline the forms of abuse
You will need: Manila paper, Textbook or notes from the teacher
1. Brainstorm forms of child abuse the group already knows.
2. Add any form from the class list that was missed, including unauthorised transport and abuse of children with special needs.
3. Beside each form, write one sentence that says why it is wrong.
4. Write two responsibilities children have, next to two rights.

## Practice
1. Name four forms of child abuse.
2. What is child trafficking?
3. Name two rights and one responsibility of a child.

## Summary
• Children have rights to education, care and protection, and they have responsibilities.
• Abuse includes forced marriage, female genital mutilation, slavery, trafficking, child labour, sexual abuse, abuse of children with special needs, and unsafe transport.
• Abuse is a crime. Girls and boys can both be harmed.

### Answers to practice
1. Any four: early and forced marriage, female genital mutilation, slavery, child trafficking, child labour, sexual abuse, abuse of children with special needs, and unauthorised school transport.
2. Stealing or moving a child and selling them to other people, in the country or across a border.
3. Rights such as education and protection. A responsibility such as working hard at school or telling a trusted adult about harm.

PAGE 3: Lesson 2: Why child abuse happens

LESSON 2: WHY CHILD ABUSE HAPPENS
=================================

## What you will learn
• Explain causes of child abuse in the community.
• Explain how some cultural practices violate children's rights.

Curriculum outcomes: b) explain the causes of child abuse in the community

## Introduction
Abuse does not happen because a child is 'difficult' or 'unlucky'. It happens because adults make harmful choices, and sometimes because a community stays silent.

## Notes
A cause is a reason something happens. Knowing causes helps a community stop abuse. It is never an excuse for the abuse.

### Causes you should be able to explain
- Poverty: some families send children to work because they need money. Poverty is hard, but it does not make child labour lawful. Help should come in ways that keep children in school.
- Greed: some people make money by trafficking children or by using them as unpaid workers.
- Ignorance: some adults do not know that children have rights, or they believe harmful practices are required.
- Harmful cultural practices: female genital mutilation and early marriage are sometimes called tradition. A tradition that injures a child violates the child's rights. Good culture, such as songs, foods and respectful ceremonies, can continue. Harmful parts must stop.
- Discrimination: children with disabilities, or girls, or children from a poorer family, may be valued less. That unfairness is a cause of neglect and abuse.
- Poor supervision: children left alone, or sent on long journeys with strangers, are easier to harm.
- Silence: when neighbours see abuse and say nothing, the harm continues.
- Misuse of power: an older or stronger person uses fear so the child will not tell.

Gender matters in the pattern of abuse. Girls are more often targeted for female genital mutilation and early marriage. Boys are often pushed into heavy labour. Both need protection. A school that teaches only one group has not understood the causes.

Use a textbook or a lesson the teacher provides to check this list. Add a cause only if you can explain it. Do not invent stories about real families in your class.

## Key words
• cause — a reason something happens
• poverty — the condition of not having enough money for basic needs
• discrimination — treating a person worse because of who they are

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A community says a girl must leave school to marry because 'it has always been done'. Which cause is this, and why does it not justify the marriage?

Working:
1. The reason given is an old practice.
2. The practice takes away education and safety.

Answer: A harmful cultural practice. Tradition does not make a violation of child rights acceptable.

### Example 2
A child with a disability is locked in the house and not taken to school. Which causes are at work?

Working:
1. The child is treated as less important.
2. The child is hidden from school and from help.

Answer: Discrimination and abuse of a child with special needs.

## Activity: Find out the causes
You will need: Textbook or a printed handout, Exercise book
1. Use the textbook or handout to list causes of child abuse.
2. In groups, match each cause to one form of abuse. Do not use the names of real children.
3. Discuss how a harmful cultural practice can violate rights even when people call it tradition.
4. Write one way silence allows abuse to continue.

## Practice
1. State three causes of child abuse.
2. How can a cultural practice violate child rights?
3. Why is the child never to blame for being abused?

## Summary
• Causes include poverty, greed, ignorance, harmful practices, discrimination and silence.
• Calling a harmful act 'tradition' does not make it right.
• Girls and boys face different risks, and both deserve protection.

### Answers to practice
1. Any three: poverty, greed, ignorance, harmful cultural practices, discrimination, poor supervision, silence and misuse of power.
2. When it harms a child, for example by forcing marriage or female genital mutilation, it takes away safety and education.
3. Abuse is an adult's harmful choice. A child's behaviour is not a reason to harm them.

PAGE 4: Lesson 3: Effects of child abuse

LESSON 3: EFFECTS OF CHILD ABUSE
================================

## What you will learn
• Explain the effects of child abuse on the child and the community.
• Design a poster that shows those effects without shaming victims.

Curriculum outcomes: c) explain effects of child abuse in the community

## Introduction
A child who drops out to work may bring a little money this week and lose years of learning. The harm spreads from the child to the whole community.

## Notes
An effect is what follows from an action. Child abuse has effects on the body, on feelings, on school and on the community. Speak about these effects with care. Do not point at a classmate and guess what happened to them.

### Effects on the child
- Injury and poor health, including lasting injury from female genital mutilation or heavy labour
- Fear, sadness and shame, even though the child did nothing wrong
- Missing school or dropping out, so the child cannot read, write and qualify for later work
- Separation from family, especially in trafficking and slavery
- Loss of play and friendship
- Difficulty trusting adults

### Effects on the community
- More children grow up without education, so the county loses skills
- Families break apart
- Illness and injury cost the community care it could have used elsewhere
- People become afraid, and silence grows
- The community gets a reputation for being unsafe

### What a poster should do
A poster on effects should inform, not frighten for fun and not show graphic pictures of injuries. Use simple sentences such as 'Child labour keeps children out of school' and 'Forced marriage steals childhood.' Add a line of hope: 'Tell a trusted adult. Children can be protected.'

Never draw a real child's face as an example of a victim. Use symbols, such as an empty desk or a locked school gate. The aim is to make people want to stop the abuse, not to embarrass a survivor.

## Key words
• effect — what happens as a result of something
• dropout — a learner who leaves school before completing it
• survivor — a person who has lived through harm

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A boy works in a quarry every day and can no longer read the work he used to do. Which effects are these?

Working:
1. His body is at risk in the quarry.
2. His learning has stopped.

Answer: Poor health or injury, and loss of education.

### Example 2
Why should a poster avoid a graphic picture of an injury?

Working:
1. The audience is children.
2. The aim is protection, not shock or shame.

Answer: Because the poster should teach the effect clearly and point people to help, without shaming survivors.

## Activity: Posters on effects
You will need: Manila paper, Crayons
1. Discuss the effects of child abuse on a child and on a community. Do not use real names.
2. Each group chooses one form of abuse and two effects.
3. Design a poster with plain words, a symbol, and a line that tells children to seek help.
4. Display the posters and check that none of them mocks or identifies a real child.

## Practice
1. State three effects of child abuse on a child.
2. How does child labour harm the community as well as the child?
3. What should a poster about effects include besides the harm?

## Summary
• Abuse can injure the body, the feelings and the chance to learn.
• The community loses skills and safety when children are harmed.
• Posters should inform and offer help, without shaming a child.

### Answers to practice
1. Any three: injury, fear and sadness, dropping out of school, separation from family, loss of play, and difficulty trusting people.
2. The child misses education, so the community loses skills it would have gained.
3. A message of help, such as telling a trusted adult.

PAGE 5: Lesson 4: Protecting children and promoting rights

LESSON 4: PROTECTING CHILDREN AND PROMOTING RIGHTS
==================================================

## What you will learn
• Explain how to get help and how to use safe school transport.
• Take part in a school activity that promotes child rights.

Curriculum outcomes: d) desire to promote child rights and responsibilities in the school

## Introduction
Protection starts with a sentence many children find hard: telling someone. A secret that hides abuse is not a secret you must keep.

## Notes
You promote child rights when you protect yourself, protect other children, and join school activities that keep rights alive.

### How to protect yourself and others
- Tell a trusted adult: a parent, guardian, teacher, head teacher, religious leader, chief or police officer. If the first person does not help, tell another.
- You can call the Childline Kenya helpline on 116. It is free from a phone and is for reporting harm to children.
- Do not go with a stranger, even if they offer gifts, a lift or a message about your family.
- Use only school transport the school has authorised. If the usual vehicle does not come, wait with a teacher or a known adult. Do not board an unknown car or motorcycle.
- Walk with other learners when you can. Tell someone at home when you have arrived.
- Say no to secrets about touching. Safe adults do not ask children to keep harmful touching secret.
- If a friend is being kept from school, hurt, or hidden because of a disability, tell a teacher. You are helping, not betraying them.
- Do not meet an online stranger or send photos of your body.

### At school
Sing songs and recite poems that say children have a right to school and to safety. Create awareness about authorised transport: a short talk at assembly can remind learners which vehicles are allowed.

Other activities include a rights club, a poster week, welcoming learners with special needs into games, and reporting bullying. Responsibilities sit beside these rights. You respect other children's bodies and property, you come to school, and you do not laugh at a child who asks for help.

Wanting rights for others is part of good citizenship. A school that protects one group and ignores another has not finished the work.

## Key words
• trusted adult — an adult you know who has a duty to help you, such as a parent or teacher
• authorised transport — a vehicle the school has approved for carrying learners
• helpline — a telephone service you can call to report harm and get help

## Worked examples

### Example 1
The school bus does not arrive, and a stranger offers a lift. What should the learner do?

Working:
1. The stranger's vehicle is not authorised.
2. A known adult should be told.

Answer: Refuse the lift and wait with a teacher or another known adult, or use only the transport the school has approved.

### Example 2
An adult says a harmful touch must stay secret. Is that correct?

Working:
1. Harmful secrets protect the abuser.
2. A trusted adult needs to know.

Answer: No. The child should tell a trusted adult. Such a secret should not be kept.

## Activity: Rights songs and safe transport
You will need: Exercise book, Manila paper
1. Compose a short poem or song about protecting yourself and others from child abuse.
2. Recite or sing it to the class.
3. Make a notice that explains authorised school transport: which vehicle to use and what to do if it does not come.
4. Share the notice with another class so that peers hear the message.
5. Agree one action the class will take this week, such as including a learner with special needs in a game.

## Practice
1. Name three people or services a child can tell about abuse.
2. What is authorised school transport?
3. Give one responsibility that goes with the right to safety.

## Summary
• Tell a trusted adult or call 116. Do not keep a secret that hides abuse.
• Use only transport the school has approved.
• Songs, notices and inclusive games promote rights at school.

### Answers to practice
1. A parent or guardian, a teacher, the head teacher, a chief, the police, or Childline Kenya on 116.
2. A vehicle the school has approved for learners. Unknown lifts are not authorised.
3. Respect other children's bodies and tell a trusted adult when you know a child is being harmed.
pages.quiz:
REVISION QUIZ — 5.3 CHILD RIGHTS
========================================

Answer all the questions, then mark yourself on the Answers tab.

1. Child abuse is:
   A. Harming a child physically, sexually or emotionally
   B. Giving a child homework
   C. A school motto
   D. A type of trade

2. Which list contains forms of child abuse?
   A. Child labour, trafficking and forced marriage
   B. Sharing books and watering trees
   C. Peace corners and essays
   D. Voting for a class leader

3. Female genital mutilation is:
   A. A lawful school rule
   B. A harmful and unlawful practice against girls
   C. A right of every child
   D. A type of authorised transport

4. A cause of child abuse is:
   A. The child being to blame
   B. Silence, greed or a harmful cultural practice
   C. Doing homework
   D. Telling a teacher

5. Early marriage violates child rights because:
   A. It takes away education and safety
   B. It is always the child's free choice at any age
   C. It is the same as a naming ceremony
   D. It improves school attendance

6. An effect of child labour is:
   A. The child misses school and may be injured
   B. The child automatically becomes richer and safer
   C. The community gains more educated people
   D. Rights are strengthened

7. A poster about effects should:
   A. Use plain words and a help message, without shaming a real child
   B. Show a classmate's face as a victim
   C. Make injuries look exciting
   D. Hide the fact that help exists

8. If a stranger offers a lift when the school bus is late, the learner should:
   A. Get in quickly
   B. Refuse and stay with a known adult
   C. Keep it secret
   D. Pay the stranger later

9. The Childline Kenya number taught for reporting harm to children is:
   A. 999 only
   B. 116
   C. 47
   D. 100

10. Which action promotes child rights in school?
   A. Laughing at a child who reports abuse
   B. Including learners with special needs and telling a teacher about harm
   C. Sharing a private photo of a classmate
   D. Hiding a child from class

11. Why should a harmful touch not stay a secret?
pages.answers:
ANSWERS — 5.3 CHILD RIGHTS
========================================

1. A. Harming a child physically, sexually or emotionally
   Abuse is harm. Ordinary homework and safe home chores are not abuse.

2. A. Child labour, trafficking and forced marriage
   Labour that replaces school, trafficking and forced marriage are forms of abuse.

3. B. A harmful and unlawful practice against girls
   It injures girls and is against the law in Kenya.

4. B. Silence, greed or a harmful cultural practice
   Adults' choices and community silence allow abuse. The child is not the cause.

5. A. It takes away education and safety
   A child should be in school and protected, not married.

6. A. The child misses school and may be injured
   Work that replaces school damages learning and can damage the body.

7. A. Use plain words and a help message, without shaming a real child
   The poster should inform and protect, not embarrass a survivor.

8. B. Refuse and stay with a known adult
   Only authorised school transport is safe. Strangers' vehicles are not approved.

9. B. 116
   116 is the child helpline. A trusted adult should also be told.

10. B. Including learners with special needs and telling a teacher about harm
   Inclusion and reporting protect rights.

11. Because secrecy protects the person doing harm. A trusted adult needs to know so the child can be helped.
   Telling a trusted adult is protection, not disobedience.

LESSON 3: EFFECTS OF CHILD ABUSE
================================

## What you will learn
• Explain the effects of child abuse on the child and the community.

Curriculum outcomes: c) explain effects of child abuse in the community

## Introduction
A child who drops out to work may bring a little money this week and lose years of learning. The harm spreads from the child to the whole community.

## Notes
An effect is what follows from an action. Child abuse has effects on the body, on feelings, on school and on the community. Speak about these effects with care. Do not point at a classmate and guess what happened to them.

### Effects on the child
- Injury and poor health, including lasting injury from female genital mutilation or heavy labour
- Fear, sadness and shame, even though the child did nothing wrong
- Missing school or dropping out, so the child cannot read, write and qualify for later work
- Separation from family, especially in trafficking and slavery
- Loss of play and friendship
- Difficulty trusting adults

### Effects on the community
- More children grow up without education, so the county loses skills
- Families break apart
- Illness and injury cost the community care it could have used elsewhere
- People become afraid, and silence grows
- The community gets a reputation for being unsafe

### What a poster should do
A poster on effects should inform, not frighten for fun and not show graphic pictures of injuries. Use simple sentences such as 'Child labour keeps children out of school' and 'Forced marriage steals childhood.' Add a line of hope: 'Tell a trusted adult. Children can be protected.'

Never draw a real child's face as an example of a victim. Use symbols, such as an empty desk or a locked school gate. The aim is to make people want to stop the abuse, not to embarrass a survivor.

## Key words
• effect — what happens as a result of something
• dropout — a learner who leaves school before completing it
• survivor — a person who has lived through harm

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A boy works in a quarry every day and can no longer read the work he used to do. Which effects are these?

Working:
1. His body is at risk in the quarry.
2. His learning has stopped.

Answer: Poor health or injury, and loss of education.

### Example 2
Why should a poster avoid a graphic picture of an injury?

Working:
1. The audience is children.
2. The aim is protection, not shock or shame.

Answer: Because the poster should teach the effect clearly and point people to help, without shaming survivors.

## Activity: Posters on effects
You will need: Manila paper, Crayons
1. Discuss the effects of child abuse on a child and on a community. Do not use real names.
2. Each group chooses one form of abuse and two effects.
3. Design a poster with plain words, a symbol, and a line that tells children to seek help.
4. Display the posters and check that none of them mocks or identifies a real child.

## Practice
1. State three effects of child abuse on a child.
2. How does child labour harm the community as well as the child?
3. What should a poster about effects include besides the harm?

## Summary
• Abuse can injure the body, the feelings and the chance to learn.
• The community loses skills and safety when children are harmed.
• Posters should inform and offer help, without shaming a child.

### Answers to practice
1. Any three: injury, fear and sadness, dropping out of school, separation from family, loss of play, and difficulty trusting people.
2. The child misses education, so the community loses skills it would have gained.
3. A message of help, such as telling a trusted adult.

studyPages.title: Lesson 4: Protecting children and promoting rights
studyPages.body:
LESSON 4: PROTECTING CHILDREN AND PROMOTING RIGHTS
==================================================

## What you will learn
• Explain how to get help and how to use safe school transport.
• Take part in a school activity that promotes child rights.

Curriculum outcomes: d) desire to promote child rights and responsibilities in the school

## Introduction
Protection starts with a sentence many children find hard: telling someone. A secret that hides abuse is not a secret you must keep.

## Notes
You promote child rights when you protect yourself, protect other children, and join school activities that keep rights alive.

### How to protect yourself and others
- Tell a trusted adult: a parent, guardian, teacher, head teacher, religious leader, chief or police officer. If the first person does not help, tell another.
- You can call the Childline Kenya helpline on 116. It is free from a phone and is for reporting harm to children.
- Do not go with a stranger, even if they offer gifts, a lift or a message about your family.
- Use only school transport the school has authorised. If the usual vehicle does not come, wait with a teacher or a known adult. Do not board an unknown car or motorcycle.
- Walk with other learners when you can. Tell someone at home when you have arrived.
- Say no to secrets about touching. Safe adults do not ask children to keep harmful touching secret.
- If a friend is being kept from school, hurt, or hidden because of a disability, tell a teacher. You are helping, not betraying them.
- Do not meet an online stranger or send photos of your body.

### At school
Sing songs and recite poems that say children have a right to school and to safety. Create awareness about authorised transport: a short talk at assembly can remind learners which vehicles are allowed.

Other activities include a rights club, a poster week, welcoming learners with special needs into games, and reporting bullying. Responsibilities sit beside these rights. You respect other children's bodies and property, you come to school, and you do not laugh at a child who asks for help.

Wanting rights for others is part of good citizenship. A school that protects one group and ignores another has not finished the work.

## Key words
• trusted adult — an adult you know who has a duty to help you, such as a parent or teacher
• authorised transport — a vehicle the school has approved for carrying learners
• helpline — a telephone service you can call to report harm and get help

## Worked examples

### Example 1
The school bus does not arrive, and a stranger offers a lift. What should the learner do?

Working:
1. The stranger's vehicle is not authorised.
2. A known adult should be told.

Answer: Refuse the lift and wait with a teacher or another known adult, or use only the transport the school has approved.

### Example 2
An adult says a harmful touch must stay secret. Is that correct?

Working:
1. Harmful secrets protect the abuser.
2. A trusted adult needs to know.

Answer: No. The child should tell a trusted adult. Such a secret should not be kept.

## Activity: Rights songs and safe transport
You will need: Exercise book, Manila paper
1. Compose a short poem or song about protecting yourself and others from child abuse.
2. Recite or sing it to the class.
3. Make a notice that explains authorised school transport: which vehicle to use and what to do if it does not come.
4. Share the notice with another class so that peers hear the message.
5. Agree one action the class will take this week, such as including a learner with special needs in a game.

## Practice
1. Name three people or services a child can tell about abuse.
2. What is authorised school transport?
3. Give one responsibility that goes with the right to safety.

## Summary
• Tell a trusted adult or call 116. Do not keep a secret that hides abuse.
• Use only transport the school has approved.
• Songs, notices and inclusive games promote rights at school.

### Answers to practice
1. A parent or guardian, a teacher, the head teacher, a chief, the police, or Childline Kenya on 116.
2. A vehicle the school has approved for learners. Unknown lifts are not authorised.
3. Respect other children's bodies and tell a trusted adult when you know a child is being harmed.

questions.question: Child abuse is:
options: Harming a child physically, sexually or emotionally
questions.explanation: Abuse is harm. Ordinary homework and safe home chores are not abuse.

questions.question: Which list contains forms of child abuse?
options: Child labour, trafficking and forced marriage
questions.explanation: Labour that replaces school, trafficking and forced marriage are forms of abuse.

questions.question: Female genital mutilation is:
options: A harmful and unlawful practice against girls
questions.explanation: It injures girls and is against the law in Kenya.

questions.question: A cause of child abuse is:
options: Silence, greed or a harmful cultural practice
questions.explanation: Adults' choices and community silence allow abuse. The child is not the cause.

questions.question: Early marriage violates child rights because:
options: It takes away education and safety
It is always the child's free choice at any age
It is the same as a naming ceremony
questions.explanation: A child should be in school and protected, not married.

questions.question: An effect of child labour is:
options: The child misses school and may be injured
The child automatically becomes richer and safer
The community gains more educated people
questions.explanation: Work that replaces school damages learning and can damage the body.

questions.question: A poster about effects should:
options: Use plain words and a help message, without shaming a real child
Show a classmate's face as a victim
Hide the fact that help exists
questions.explanation: The poster should inform and protect, not embarrass a survivor.

questions.question: If a stranger offers a lift when the school bus is late, the learner should:
options: Refuse and stay with a known adult
questions.explanation: Only authorised school transport is safe. Strangers' vehicles are not approved.

questions.question: The Childline Kenya number taught for reporting harm to children is:
questions.explanation: 116 is the child helpline. A trusted adult should also be told.

questions.question: Which action promotes child rights in school?
options: Laughing at a child who reports abuse
Including learners with special needs and telling a teacher about harm
Sharing a private photo of a classmate

questions.question: Why should a harmful touch not stay a secret?
questions.answer: Because secrecy protects the person doing harm. A trusted adult needs to know so the child can be helped.
questions.explanation: Telling a trusted adult is protection, not disobedience.
